title: Global Payments Report 2026: The Burden of Proof
gist: BCG's 2026 payments outlook shows global payments revenue growth decelerating to ~5% CAGR through 2030 (from ~8% a decade ago) even as public-market multiples have already collapsed, while digital assets, AI/agentic commerce, and payments-sovereignty fragmentation (BRICS Pay, mBridge, digital euro, CIPS) are simultaneously reshaping who captures the value.

insights.claim: Public-market multiples for payments companies have compressed so far since 2022 that a company growing revenue 20% annually with 50% EBITDA margins can still trade at only 12x forward EV/EBITDA.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Signals a structural re-rating, not a cyclical dip — investors should not assume high growth alone restores historical multiples for payments names.
insights.quote: A payments company can now grow at 20% annually, post 50% EBITDA margins, and still trade at only 12 times forward EV/EBITDA.
insights.locator: Since 2022, public-market multiples have fallen sharply

insights.claim: Global payments revenue will grow from almost $2.0 trillion in 2025 to nearly $2.6 trillion by 2030, a ~5% CAGR that is 2 points below the prior six-year rate and well under the ~8% growth the industry saw for much of the past decade.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: A secular growth downshift, not noise — models and valuations built on historical payments growth rates need resetting.
insights.locator: The Next Five Years Will See Meaningfully Slower Growth

insights.claim: Transaction-related payments revenue will keep growing 6% annually through 2030 on digital adoption and inflation, but non-transaction revenue (the larger pool) will slow to 5% growth as the boost from higher interest rates fades.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive deposit/float income was propping up payments revenue growth; as that tailwind normalizes, the larger revenue pool decelerates first.
insights.locator: Transaction-related revenues will grow by 6% annually

insights.claim: North America remains the largest payments revenue pool at $842 billion in 2025 and will keep growing at roughly 5% annually, in line with the global average rather than leading it.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Scale leadership no longer implies growth leadership; incremental payments growth is shifting to smaller, faster-growing regions.
insights.locator: North America is by far the largest revenue pool

insights.claim: In Asia-Pacific ($515 billion revenue pool), payments revenue growth will trail transaction volume growth because lower-monetizing rails like India's UPI are gaining share over higher-margin credit card volume.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Volume growth headlines in APAC payments overstate monetization; investors should track revenue-per-transaction, not just transaction counts.

insights.claim: Latin America ($200 billion, growing 7% to ~$300 billion by 2030) and the Middle East and Africa ($98 billion, growing 8% to ~$150 billion) will be the fastest-growing payments regions, driven by instant-payment rail scaling (Brazil, Argentina) and cash-to-digital migration respectively.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: These smaller, higher-growth regions are where payments providers can still find above-average organic growth as mature markets decelerate.
insights.locator: Latin America and the Middle East and Africa are smaller but will grow fastest

themes.theme: Digital assets and tokenization reshaping settlement

insights.claim: As of mid-2026, crypto market cap stood at roughly $2.3 trillion, with stablecoins at $260 billion and tokenized real-world assets on public chains at $38 billion, and tokenized assets could reach 9%-16% of global investable assets by 2035 under a high-growth scenario.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Even the smaller tokenized-RWA segment is already large enough to be reshaping issuance, custody, servicing, and settlement infrastructure ahead of any mass-adoption scenario.

insights.claim: Stablecoins are still used primarily for crypto trading today, but adoption is spreading into real-economy payments where legacy rails are expensive or slow — cross-border business payments, treasury transfers, platform payouts, remittances, FX settlement, and tokenized fund operations.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Watch cross-border B2B and treasury flows as the next stablecoin adoption front, ahead of consumer payments.
insights.locator: Today, the primary use for stablecoins is in crypto trading

insights.claim: J.P. Morgan, Citi, HSBC, and DBS have tested or launched tokenized deposits for corporate clients to keep funds on-balance-sheet within existing regulation, but the product won't create scalable value until it can move between banks, and cross-bank interoperability is still at an early piloting stage.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Tokenized-deposit initiatives are more defensive positioning than a near-term revenue driver until interoperability is solved.

insights.claim: If digital assets capture a larger share of cross-border payments and cash management, banks risk losing float income, deposits, and fee revenue from some of their highest-margin transaction flows, even though BCG's own view (from its Future of Digital Assets report) is that legacy and tokenized rails will coexist for years rather than one fully displacing the other.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Coexistence doesn't mean today's incumbent revenue shares hold — banks that don't secure wallets/custody/on-off-ramp capability risk disintermediation even in a coexistence scenario.
insights.quote: That doesn’t mean that today’s market positions will hold.
insights.locator: But that doesn't mean that today's market positions will hold

themes.theme: Public markets are repricing payments business models

insights.claim: Buy-now-pay-later providers, digital-assets companies, and card issuers have outperformed the S&P 500 in recent years, while acquirers and processors have posted negative returns and networks have lagged the broader market.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: The payments sell-off is not uniform — capital is rotating away from commoditized processing/acquiring toward issuing and digital-asset-adjacent models with clearer product differentiation.
insights.locator: Public Equity Markets Are Reordering the Sector

insights.claim: Investors are no longer rewarding scale on its own; they favor 'share takers' over 'share donors' with product advantage and operating leverage, and even a small number of consistent share gainers have faced valuation overhangs over the past 12-24 months.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Growth and share gains alone no longer guarantee multiple support — screen for durable product moats, not just market-share trajectory, when evaluating payments equities.
insights.locator: They pay close attention to share takers versus share donors

themes.theme: Structural pressure on core payments business models

insights.claim: Acquiring remains burdened by excess capacity and legacy infrastructure, while in issuing, growth is concentrating among the largest scaled providers (who can invest in rewards, data, and new monetization) and fast-growing fintechs, with the strongest fintechs in commercial cards and B2B payments becoming acquisition targets for larger incumbents.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Expect continued consolidation as incumbents acquire share-gaining fintechs in commercial cards/B2B rather than build in-house.
insights.locator: Competition is intensifying in core businesses

insights.claim: AI is raising the payments industry's performance bar by lowering the cost to serve clients, manage risk, and handle exceptions, while agentic commerce could reshape the entire online transaction journey from discovery and authentication through payment choice.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Agentic commerce is a potential structural disruptor to merchant/consumer payment-choice economics, not just a cost-efficiency tool — worth tracking who controls the agent-driven checkout layer.
insights.locator: AI is raising the performance bar

insights.claim: By June 2026, 137 countries had 24-7 instant payment access, with massive scale already reached: Brazil's Pix processed nearly 80 billion transactions in 2025, India's UPI processed 23.2 billion transactions in May 2026 alone, Colombia's Bre-B handled over 670 million transactions in its first six months, and 36 African instant payment systems across 31 countries processed 64 billion transactions worth nearly $2 trillion in 2024.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Domestic instant-payment rails have already reached scale sufficient to structurally erode card-network transaction volumes in these markets.
insights.locator: As of June 2026, individuals and businesses in 137 countries

insights.claim: Governments are actively building cross-border interoperability among domestic rails — Poland's Blik has entered Romania and Slovakia, Brazil has expanded Pix across its border with Argentina, and the BIS-led Project Nexus aims to connect Asian instant-payment systems covering 1.7 billion people — while the EU has extended interchange fee caps and forced Apple to open tap-to-pay to competing wallets.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Regulatory moves (interchange caps, forced wallet access) are actively compressing the fee economics that global card networks and Apple's payments ecosystem have historically captured.

insights.claim: BRICS Pay aims to link members' payment rails directly, bypassing SWIFT and dollar settlement, with a business-to-business rollout targeted for the second half of 2026, while mBridge already settles cross-border transactions in central bank digital currencies among China, Hong Kong, Thailand, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia — though neither system is close to rivaling SWIFT's reach and BRICS members haven't uniformly committed.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: De-dollarization payment infrastructure is now an explicit design goal rather than a side effect, worth monitoring even though it's not yet a near-term threat to SWIFT's dominance.
insights.quote: sovereignty and de-dollarization are now explicit design goals rather than side effects
insights.locator: A more overtly geopolitical version of this dynamic is emerging in BRICS countries

insights.claim: Europe and China are pursuing divergent tokenized-money strategies — the EU approved opening negotiations on digital euro legislation in July 2026 (explicitly framed by the ECB as protection against non-European card schemes and dollar stablecoins) alongside a bank consortium building the euro-stablecoin Qivalis, while China bans dollar-linked stablecoins, has let banks pay interest on digital yuan wallets since January 2026, and has grown its CIPS messaging system as a SWIFT alternative for trade with sanctioned or sanctions-wary counterparties.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/inderpreet-batra
insights.so_what: Regional monetary blocs are building parallel, non-dollar settlement rails as explicit sovereignty policy — a multi-year theme for currency/settlement infrastructure investors to track, not a near-term dollar-displacement event.
